A source-grounded visual reading

Gonka’s decentralized AI thesis, made explicit.

The paper proposes a network that measures each provider’s AI-relevant compute in a short contest, converts that measurement into voting and work weight, then uses the rest of the cycle for real inference and training.

1
The key move Security does not occupy every GPU continuously. A periodic “Sprint” snapshots who controls how much transformer-class compute. That snapshot governs the network until the next Sprint.
Enter the system
≈10 min Illustrative Sprint duration paper p. 6
1 / 900 Target hit rate per nonce paper p. 18
1–10% Claimed task repetition after spot checks paper p. 8
20% Inference revenue reserved for training paper p. 11
01 / Thesis

The paper is solving two different wastes.

The argument begins with centralized AI clouds, then turns to decentralized networks. The paper treats both as misaligned, but for different reasons. Centralized systems concentrate pricing and control. Existing crypto systems spend too much on consensus, capital subsidies or duplicate verification instead of delivering AI work. pp. 1–4

Paper’s diagnosis

Centralized cloud

  • Large providers can charge smaller buyers more than strategic enterprise customers.
  • Developers remain subject to platform policies, monitoring and withdrawal of service.
  • Buying hardware can lower unit cost, but it sacrifices elasticity when demand varies.
Efficient operation, concentrated market power
Paper’s diagnosis

Traditional decentralization

  • Proof-of-Work continuously burns compute to establish majority control.
  • Proof-of-Stake moves the cost from electricity to paid-up capital.
  • Decentralized AI often repeats expensive tasks to make results trustworthy.
Distributed control, high security and verification overhead
Proposed design

Periodic proof of compute

  • Measure transformer-class throughput only during a short, synchronized Sprint.
  • Keep the resulting compute weights active for the rest of the cycle.
  • Use those weights for consensus, job assignment, audits and rewards.
The intended result: security overhead becomes a small duty cycle
The decisive assumption: a short benchmark can produce a trustworthy snapshot of each Host’s continuing, AI-relevant capacity. If the snapshot can be rented, gamed or decoupled from later service, the system’s security and workload allocation both weaken.
02 / System map

One measurement drives four powers.

The Sprint result is not merely a block-production score. The proposal reuses it as a common accounting unit for governance influence, task share, validation duty and compensation. This is why the benchmark matters so much. Any bias in the benchmark propagates through the whole network. pp. 5–7

Consensus Weight says whose signature counts.

Hosts representing more than half of active compute weight can confirm blocks and disputed results, under the paper’s honest-majority assumption.

Allocation Weight says how much work a Host should receive.

The scheduler attempts to keep utilization and reward share proportional to demonstrated capacity.

Obligation Weight also creates a duty.

A Host must execute its proportional workload and perform its proportional validation share. Missing either can reduce or erase rewards.

Consequence Benchmark quality becomes constitutional.

If Sprint performance does not track production performance, the wrong Hosts gain control, jobs and revenue at the same time.

03 / Sprint

A transformer forward pass becomes a lottery ticket.

Every Host receives the same Sprint seed, reconstructs the same compact Transformer and repeatedly tries nonce-derived inputs. An output is a “proof” only when its final vector lands close enough to a common target vector. More attempts per minute produce more valid hits, so the hit count estimates compute throughput. pp. 17–20

Mechanism
Generate a shared Sprint seed.The seed must be unknown before the starting gun and identical for every Host. It initializes the model and target.
Bind each Host to its public key.A Host-specific Node Seed makes proofs attributable and prevents one Host from submitting another Host’s nonces.
Turn each nonce into an input sequence.Nonce + Node Seed + Sprint Seed deterministically create the Transformer input.
Run the Transformer.The paper specifies 64 layers, 128 heads, embedding width 512, feed-forward width 8192, vocabulary 8192 and sequence length 4.
Scramble and measure the last vector.A nonce-dependent coordinate permutation is applied, then Euclidean /juːˈklɪdiən/ distance to the target is computed.
Reveal only winning nonces.The threshold is tuned so one attempt wins about once in 900 tries. Validators rerun those winners and count valid proofs.
d(x,t) = √ Σi=1512 (xi − ti)²
valid proof when d(x,t) < τ, with P(hit) ≈ 1/900
Why it measures speed

Each ticket costs a real forward pass. Faster transformer hardware prints more tickets before time expires.

Why validation is cheaper

The Host does every attempt. A validator only reruns the small set of claimed winners, roughly one pass per 900 attempts.

What it does not prove

It does not prove the Host will keep the hardware online, serve long contexts well or behave honestly after Sprint.

04 / What the math implies

Shorter Sprints save energy, but make voting weights noisier.

If a Host completes n attempts and each has hit probability p, then the hit count is approximately binomial. The expected count is np; its standard deviation is about √np. Relative noise therefore falls only as 1/√hits. The design must choose enough hits to rank Hosts reliably without making validation expensive. The paper states the threshold, but does not present this calibration.

At 90,000 attempts
100

Expected hits

One-standard-deviation relative noise is about 10%. A 95% band is roughly ±19.6%. Two similarly sized Hosts can swap rank by chance.

At 900,000 attempts
1k

Expected hits

One-standard-deviation relative noise falls to 3.2%. The approximate 95% band is ±6.2%. Better, but still material for close competitors.

At 9,000,000 attempts
10k

Expected hits

One-standard-deviation relative noise is about 1%. Stable measurement now requires validators to replay around 10,000 winning passes per Host.

Design tradeoff: decreasing the hit probability makes proofs cheaper to validate but increases sampling noise. Increasing Sprint duration improves measurement precision but spends more GPU time on a synthetic security benchmark rather than user work.
05 / The duty cycle

Measure briefly. Work for the rest of the epoch.

The paper suggests a short Sprint, perhaps ten minutes, repeated on a longer cycle that might correspond to roughly 24 hours after tuning. The weight from the last Sprint remains active until the next one. Rewards accumulate during the cycle and are released only after workload and audit obligations are satisfied. pp. 5–8

Starting gun

1. Random seed

Hosts jointly establish an unpredictable Sprint seed. No one should be able to prepare model outputs in advance.

≈10 minutes

2. Sprint

Every Host runs the same AI-shaped nonce search. Winning nonces establish the next compute-weight distribution.

Most of cycle

3. Useful work

Hosts serve inference, validate peers and potentially participate in training. Work share follows PoC weight.

Continuous

4. Escrow + audit

Rewards remain pending. Random checks and user challenges can trigger majority re-verification.

Cycle end

5. Settle + reset

Honest Hosts receive rewards. Fraud can erase the cycle’s earnings and reset reputation. A new Sprint replaces the old weight.

Why the snapshot exists

Continuous PoW would defeat the purpose.

The whole proposal depends on reusing a short compute measurement across a much longer useful-work window. The security cost is approximately Sprint duration divided by cycle duration, plus validation and chain overhead.

Snapshot risk

Capacity can disappear after the photograph.

A Host could rent GPUs for Sprint, earn weight, then release them. The paper’s workload-proof penalties and GNK collateral are intended to make this unattractive, but the exact anti-rental economics and availability tests are not specified.

06 / Verification

Spot checks turn honesty into an economic bet.

The network does not replay every inference. It pseudo-randomly selects some work for validation, holds the entire cycle’s rewards in reserve and confiscates them if fraud is found. The deterrent comes from repeated exposure: a Host cannot know which tasks will be checked. pp. 7–10

Probability of detection

One audit is weak. Repeated chances compound.

If each cheated task has independent audit probability q, and a Host cheats on m tasks, the probability of at least one detection is:

P(caught) = 1 − (1 − q)m
63.4%chance of at least one detection

This is the basic deterrence math, not a complete security model. Audits can be correlated, validators can collude and some attacks may be hard to classify.

Economic condition

Slashing must dominate the savings from cheating.

A rational Host compares the extra cost it avoids by using a smaller model, skipping work or returning manipulated output against the risk of losing escrowed rewards and reputation.

Expected cheating value
= (1 − Pcaught) × extra savings
− Pcaught × forfeited escrow
− future reputation loss
Detection probability as cheating repeats

The paper describes full-cycle forfeiture, bounties and user-triggered disputes, but it does not provide a quantitative parameter set proving that every profitable attack becomes unprofitable.

Model substitution

Use a cheaper or smaller model, return a plausible answer and collect the full fee. Exact detection requires a concrete output-equivalence test.

Selective cheating

Cheat only on requests that seem hard to audit or low-value. Independent uniform spot checks may not match the real risk distribution.

Verifier collusion

An executor and assigned validators can cooperate. The paper relies on weighted majority re-verification and assumes most compute weight is honest.

Manipulated content

A Host can insert advertising, misinformation or policy-biased text. Determining “correct” generative output is often subjective rather than mathematical.

Challenge spam

User-paid reports create accountability, but fee and bounty calibration must prevent harassment, denial of service and bounty farming.

Numerical variance

Different hardware and kernels can produce small output differences. The paper explicitly treats verification as statistical, with thresholds and majority rechecks still to be defined.

07 / Reputation

Trust is earned by lowering your audit tax.

New executors begin with zero reputation and may have every task checked. In the high-volume regime, the paper proposes a linear reduction from 100% validation to 1% over N days or epochs, with a default example of 30. Fraud resets reputation to zero. pp. 9, 22–23

Published high-volume curve
v(d) = 1 − 0.99 × MIN(d, N) / N    with N = 30
Validation probability over reputation age

The paper separately says low volume, at 100 or fewer requests per day or epoch, validates every task. It describes a linear medium-volume adjustment but does not give a complete formula.

Executor economics

Validation is paid from the executor’s reward.

When a task is checked, the reward is split between the executor and validator or validators. Lower validation frequency therefore means higher expected take-home reward.

New Host
50%
Day 15
74.8%
Day 30+
99.5%

These are expected executor shares if each audited task is split 50/50 and the high-volume validation curve applies.

Implication: reputation reduces network overhead, but it also gives incumbents a large margin advantage over new Hosts. A robust identity and reputation-transfer policy becomes economically important.
08 / The hard trust problem

AI output is not a block hash.

A blockchain transaction can often be replayed exactly. Generative inference is harder. Sampling, floating-point order, quantization and kernels can yield different tokens or logits across hardware. The paper recognizes this and proposes statistical judgments plus majority re-verification, but the acceptance test remains underspecified. pp. 8–9

01

Flag

A random validator or user challenge marks a result as suspicious. One mismatch is not enough to declare fraud.

02

Re-run

Additional Hosts representing a majority of compute weight reproduce or statistically compare the result.

03

Threshold

The system tolerates a limited error rate so hardware variance does not punish honest Hosts for one deviation.

04

Settle

Consistent outliers can lose the cycle’s rewards and reputation. Honest differences must remain below a model-specific boundary.

What can be made deterministic

Fixed model, fixed prompt, fixed seed, fixed decoding.

Constrained inference can be close to reproducible when the protocol pins weights, quantization, tokenizer, sampling parameters and numerical implementation. The more freedom a Host has, the harder exact verification becomes.

What still needs a specification

Equivalence, tolerances and adversarial edge cases.

The white paper does not define whether validators compare exact tokens, logits, embeddings, task-specific scores or human judgments. Each option changes cost, false-positive risk and the attacks that remain possible.

09 / Inference product

The user experience is meant to look ordinary.

Developers submit requests through an API similar to centralized model APIs. The network chooses a Host running an approved open model, returns the output and accounts for cost. Underneath that familiar surface sit weighted routing, escrow, validation and dispute handling. pp. 10–11

Hosts

Provide GPUs, execute inference, verify peers and receive both protocol emissions and user-paid work rewards.

Developers

Choose supported open models, submit requests and set maximum compute cost through an API.

Users

Generate demand and can trigger paid challenges when output appears incorrect or malicious.

Product advantage

Open model access without one cloud gatekeeper.

The network could make capacity and pricing more contestable while allowing developers to avoid a single provider’s model policy, account controls and margin structure.

Product gaps

Privacy, latency and service levels are not solved by decentralization alone.

The routing scheme hides a user’s IP from the executor through an intermediary Host, but the paper does not provide prompt confidentiality, trusted execution, end-to-end encryption for model inputs, latency guarantees or availability guarantees.

10 / Decentralized training

Train locally for a long time, synchronize occasionally.

The training plan combines DiLoCo, on-chain coordination, proof-of-learning style audits and model sharding. DiLoCo reduces bandwidth by letting Hosts take many local optimizer steps before an outer synchronization. The chain replaces a central rendezvous coordinator. pp. 11, 24–26

DiLoCo pattern
Host A

Many local AdamW steps on assigned data or model path.

Host B

Works independently instead of exchanging gradients every step.

Host C

Commits selected state hashes for later verification.

Host D

May train only a model shard or Mixture-of-Experts path.

Periodic outer synchronization
On-chain rendezvous and rank assignment coordinate aggregation. Bulk model state remains off-chain.
Proof of learning

Commit the before and after state.

At pseudo-random steps, a Host preserves previous weights, current weights and optimizer state, then puts hashes on-chain. Validators can demand the off-chain artifacts and check whether the transition is plausible.

Validator oversight

Check the checkers.

Validator judgments remain on-chain. Honeypot submissions and re-validation are intended to reveal lazy or colluding validators.

Sharding

Do not require every Host to hold the whole training model.

The proposal points to MoE and path-composition research so each Host can train a subset of parameters while the combined model is much larger.

What this buys

Lower communication and no permanent central coordinator.

Periodic synchronization makes geographic distribution more plausible. On-chain coordination can survive individual coordinator failure and creates an auditable schedule.

What remains research

Validation cost, data integrity and integrated scaling.

Checking optimizer transitions can itself be expensive. A valid-looking step can still use poisoned data or optimize the wrong objective. The paper provides an architecture direction, not end-to-end empirical results for untrusted large-scale training.

11 / Economics

Users pay for work. Emissions subsidize the network.

The paper describes two reward streams denominated in GNK: protocol-minted “Reward Coins” allocated by Proof of Compute, and developer-paid “Work Coins” for actual inference. Emissions decline in a Bitcoin-style schedule. Twenty percent of inference revenue is reserved for future training. pp. 11–12

Revenue sources

GNK inflow

Protocol emissionReward Coins
Developer paymentsWork Coins
Distribution

Where value goes

Execution + validationHosts
Inference revenue reserve20% training
The subsidy effect

Cheap service is partly paid by token issuance.

Early emissions can let customers pay less than the full hardware cost while Hosts still earn enough. The cost does not disappear. It is transferred to token dilution and whoever values or buys GNK.

Demand dependency

Scarcity is not demand.

A declining emission schedule does not mechanically raise token value. Host economics improve only if real usage, fee revenue or external token demand grows fast enough as issuance falls.

Gas-like execution

Running out of compute can consume the payment.

The proposed EIP-1559-inspired system lets developers specify a maximum price. If resources are exhausted before completion, the transaction is canceled and spent coins are not refunded.

Cold-start tension: low request volume causes more validation and more dummy work, which raises cost. Lower prices may depend on token subsidy, while token value depends on future demand. A launch plan must break that loop with committed workloads, subsidized liquidity or both.
12 / Governance

Compute earns influence. Capital unlocks most of it.

Governance is presented as compute-weighted rather than coin-holder voting. In practice, only 20% of a Host’s PoC-derived weight is active automatically. The remaining 80% requires GNK collateral. This is a deliberate hybrid: recent compute establishes capacity; locked capital adds economic commitment. paper p. 13

20%active by default
80% needs GNK collateral
Compute earnedCapital activated
33.4%
Quorum

At least this fraction of active PoC-weighted power must participate or the proposal is invalid.

>50%
Majority threshold

More than half of non-abstaining weighted votes must approve.

33.4%
Veto threshold

No-with-veto votes at this level force rejection even when ordinary yes votes would otherwise win.

Motivation and consequence

Collateral limits hit-and-run governance, but reintroduces wealth.

Requiring GNK makes it costly to rent compute briefly and govern without exposure. It also favors large, well-capitalized Hosts. The design is not pure “one compute unit, one vote”; it is compute-weighted influence gated by capital.

13 / Claim audit

The mechanisms are clearer than the evidence.

The white paper is an architectural proposal. It gives enough detail to understand the intended system, but not enough empirical or economic evidence to establish its strongest cost, utilization, security and scaling claims. The table below separates each claim from the mechanism offered and the missing proof.

Claim
Mechanism in the paper
Evidence still needed
Almost 100% meaningful compute

The paper contrasts Gonka with continuous PoW and high staking rewards.

Short Sprint + 1–10% spot checks

Most of the cycle is reserved for inference or training.

Measured end-to-end overhead

Sprint, dummy tasks, proof replay, disputes, chain coordination, idle capacity and failed jobs all consume resources.

Lower cost than centralized clouds

The paper suggests subsidies and competition can reduce prices materially.

Open provider market + token emission

Hosts compete and protocol rewards offset hardware cost.

A complete cost model

Hardware, power, bandwidth, token volatility, audit cost, developer acquisition, latency and margin need benchmarked numbers.

Fair compute-weighted representation

Sprint proof count approximates transformer throughput.

Random model + hit-count PoW

Unpredictable parameters block precomputation.

Correlation with production work

The benchmark must predict real throughput across models, context lengths, quantization, batching and hardware classes.

Trustworthy inference with little repetition

Random audits, majority rechecks, escrow and reputation deter fraud.

Probabilistic verification

Repeated cheating raises the chance of losing the entire cycle reward.

Attack-calibrated parameters

Audit selection, output equivalence, slashing amount, false-positive rate and collusion resistance need adversarial testing.

Large-scale decentralized training

DiLoCo, on-chain coordination, proof of learning and sharding are combined.

Low-frequency sync + state commitments

Hosts train locally and expose selected artifacts on demand.

An integrated prototype

The paper does not report a full untrusted multi-Host training run, validation overhead, convergence or poisoning resistance.

Censorship resistance

Compute is distributed among independent Hosts.

No single cloud operator

Open-source models can run across a global network.

Control-plane analysis

Model admission, software releases, governance capture, sanctions, gateway concentration and data availability can still centralize control.

Internal specification check

The stated architecture does not obviously total 2.3 billion parameters.

Appendix B states 64 layers, model width 512, feed-forward width 8192, vocabulary 8192 and about 2.3B parameters. Under a conventional dense Transformer calculation:

Attention per layer4 × 512² = 1.05M
Two-matrix FFN per layer2 × 512 × 8192 = 8.39M
64 layers + token embeddings≈ 608M
With a three-matrix gated FFN≈ 877M
Paper’s stated total≈ 2.3B
Why this matters

The benchmark needs an exact, reproducible reference implementation.

Parameter count determines memory traffic, forward-pass cost and validator load. Also, 128 heads with width 512 implies a head dimension of 4 under the standard split, which is unusual. Either omitted components, nonstandard head dimensions or one of the published numbers must be clarified. pp. 17–18

Benchmark fidelity

Sequence length 4 mostly measures dense matrix multiplication.

It barely exercises long-context attention, KV-cache traffic, memory capacity, interconnect or serving scheduler behavior. A Host can be excellent at Sprint and mediocre at the workload developers actually buy.

Randomness protocol

The paper names good primitives, not a finished beacon.

Threshold cryptography and timed commit-reveal address manipulation, but liveness, withholding, bias, membership changes and recovery need a concrete protocol and adversarial analysis.

Concentration

One-compute-unit-one-vote can still centralize.

If a few operators own most relevant GPUs, they receive most governance weight, jobs, validation duty and emissions. Sybil resistance does not guarantee a broad provider distribution.

14 / Verdict

A strong architecture thesis, not yet a proven protocol.

The paper’s useful insight is sharper than the slogan “make PoW useful.” Sprint itself is synthetic security work. The real innovation is to make that work short, AI-shaped and reusable as the network’s capacity ledger, then spend most GPU time on customer work.

+

Strongest idea

Separate capacity attestation from continuous service. A periodic AI-aligned benchmark can be a cleaner basis for assigning jobs and influence than either passive stake or a generic hash race.

!

Hardest problem

Verify non-deterministic inference and untrusted training cheaply enough that attacks are unprofitable, while honest numerical differences do not trigger slashing.

≈

Current status

The document is a system design and research program. It is not yet a cost proof, a security proof, a production benchmark or evidence that the integrated network trains frontier-scale models.

The paper should be read as a proposed operating system for a GPU marketplace: Sprint measures capacity, PoC weight allocates power, escrow and spot checks police execution, reputation reduces audit cost, token emission funds the cold start, and DiLoCo-based training is the long-term research layer. The design is coherent at the architectural level. Its viability rests on four unproven bridges: Sprint-to-real-work correlation, robust output verification, anti-concentration economics and an integrated training demonstration.
